title: Insulation resistance over ten minutes: IR, DAR and PI

interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is the IR curve flattening, and PI and DAR falling towards 1, when you step the insulation from dry to wet, while the 1-minute reading still clears the client's figure.
interactive.title: Ten minutes on one core
interactive.whatAmILookingAt:
Thirteen screens, with Back and Continue, on the insulation resistance test and the PI and DAR ratios.

Screen 1, Do you still have it? The question: "One core reads 2.0 GΩ at 1 minute and 6.0 GΩ at 10 minutes. What is its PI, and how does it rate?" Three choices, in this order: "0.33, poor"; "3.00, okay"; "4.0, okay". Right, the second: "Still there." Then the working: "PI = R10 ÷ R1 = 6.0 ÷ 2.0 = 3.00. That sits in the 2 to 4 band, okay." A last line names the slips: 0.33 is the ratio upside down, and 4.0 is how far the reading rose. Then two buttons. Refresh the why goes to screen 2, and Skip to the practice goes to screen 8. Wrong, the first: "That is the ratio upside down, 2.0 ÷ 6.0. Put the 10-minute reading on top. A healthy core's PI comes out above 1." Wrong, the third: "That is the rise, 6.0 − 2.0 GΩ. PI is a ratio. Divide the 10-minute reading by the 1-minute reading." Then the right working, and on to screen 2.

Screen 2, What it is for. "The IR test puts a steady d.c. voltage between a core and its screen. It is the same test you do on an installation, read over 10 minutes instead of once. The tester measures the tiny current that gets through the XLPE and shows it as a resistance. It answers one question: is the insulation dry and clean, at low stress? It runs after core resistance and before the sheath test. On String B it runs at 5 kV d.c. That is the client's choice, and a practice value here." The picture shows one core in cross-section. The copper is in the middle, the XLPE round it and the screen outside. The tester sits beside it, red lead on the screen and black lead on the core. Small arrows cross the XLPE from screen to core, labelled "nanoamps". In red, what goes wrong if it is skipped: "Damp or dirty insulation goes on to the high-voltage tests unseen. So does a core that passes on one reading but leaks steadily."

Screen 3, The why: three currents. "The current the tester sees has three parts. A charging current fills the cable's capacitance and dies away in seconds. An absorption current flows while the insulation slowly polarises. Charge inside the plastic shifts into line with the field, and that slow shift is a current. It dies away over minutes. A leakage current runs through the insulation and stays. The tester shows voltage ÷ current. So as the first two die away, the reading climbs. Water or dirt adds leakage, and leakage does not die away. It swamps the absorption, so the reading hardly climbs." The picture is a sketch of one core at 5 kV over 10 minutes. The top graph shows resistance against time, from 0 to 10 minutes. Its scale runs from 1 to 100 GΩ, and each mark is ten times the last. A caption: "A sketch, from one simple rule and practice values." Marks at 30 s, 1 minute and 10 minutes carry the readings. The graph underneath shows current against time, in nanoamps. The absorption current falls away above a flat band of leakage current. The charging current is drawn as a spike in the first few seconds, off the top of the scale. A stepper named Insulation has three settings: Dry, Damp and Wet. It opens on Dry. The sketch's rule: 1 ÷ R = 1 ÷ R∞ + 0.061 × e^(−t ÷ 70 s), with R in GΩ. R∞ is the steady leakage as a resistance: 64 GΩ dry, 10 GΩ damp and 2.4 GΩ wet. The readouts show the readings at 30 s, 1 minute and 10 minutes. Then come DAR = R60s ÷ R30s and PI = R10 ÷ R1, each a plain number in its readout. Their bands in words sit on one line under the readouts, so they fit on a phone. Each is worked from the readings shown before it. Dry: 18.1, 24.1 and 64.0 GΩ. DAR 1.33, satisfactory. PI 2.66, okay. The leakage is 78 nA. The absorption falls from 199 nA at 30 s to 129 nA at 1 minute. By 10 minutes it is under 0.1 nA. Damp: 7.16, 7.94 and 10.00 GΩ. DAR 1.11, inadequate. PI 1.26, questionable. The leakage is 500 nA. Wet: 2.19, 2.26 and 2.40 GΩ. DAR 1.03, inadequate. PI 1.06, questionable. The leakage is 2083 nA. The 129 nA of absorption at 1 minute is lost under it. A dashed line marks 1 GΩ, the client's figure at 1 minute. All three cores clear it. The prompt: "Step from Dry to Wet." Read: the dry core climbs from 18.1 GΩ at 30 s to 64.0 GΩ at 10 minutes, a PI of 2.66. In the wet core, a steady 2083 nA of leakage swamps the absorption. It reads 2.19, 2.26 and 2.40 GΩ, a PI of 1.06. Both clear 1 GΩ at 1 minute. Against the client's 1 GΩ alone, only the climb tells them apart. Still: the Dry and Wet curves are drawn together, each with its readings, DAR and PI.

Screen 4, The why: a ratio ignores the weather. "A single reading swings with temperature. As a rule of thumb, insulation resistance halves for every 10 °C rise and doubles for every 10 °C fall.[^1] So a reading on a warm day can look worse than last month's, with nothing wrong. PI and DAR take two readings close together, on the same cable, at the same temperature. Warmth pulls both down together, so the ratio barely moves." The picture shows the dry core from screen 3 as two bars beside a thermometer. One bar is the 1-minute reading and one the 10-minute reading. Assume it was read at 20 °C, where it reads 24.1 and 64.0 GΩ. The sketch assumes both readings fall alike. The scale along the bottom runs from 1 to 1000 GΩ, and each mark is ten times the last, so the gap between the two bar ends shows the PI. A Cable temperature slider runs from 0 to 40 °C in steps of 1 °C, opening at 20 °C. Each reading is its 20 °C figure × 2^((20 − t) ÷ 10), shown to 1 place. There are three readouts. At 1 minute and At 10 minutes are in GΩ. PI is to 2 places, worked from the unrounded readings. At 0 °C: 96.4 and 256.0 GΩ. At 10 °C: 48.2 and 128.0 GΩ. At 12 °C, String B's temperature: 42.0 and 111.4 GΩ. At 30 °C: 12.1 and 32.0 GΩ. At 40 °C: 6.0 and 16.0 GΩ. The PI reads 2.66 at every setting. The prompt: "Drag the temperature from 20 °C up to 40 °C." Read: at 20 °C the core reads 24.1 GΩ at 1 minute. At 40 °C the same sound core reads 6.0 GΩ, a quarter as much. Both bars slide down together, and the gap between their ends stays the same. Its PI stays at 2.66 the whole way. Still: the bars at 40 °C, with the 20 °C bars drawn faintly behind.

Screen 5, Check. "Two cores of one cable both read 3.00 GΩ at 1 minute, well over the client's 1 GΩ. At 10 minutes, core X reads 3.20 GΩ and core Y reads 9.00 GΩ. Which core has a steady leakage, such as moisture?" Choices: "Core X"; "Core Y"; "Neither: both pass 1 GΩ". Right, the first: "X's reading hardly climbs. PI = 3.20 ÷ 3.00 = 1.07, questionable. Most of X's current is steady leakage, and leakage does not die away. Y climbs to a PI of 9.00 ÷ 3.00 = 3.00, okay, as its absorption current dies." Wrong, the second: "Y's reading changed the most, and that is the healthy sign. Its absorption current died away and left only a small leakage." Wrong, the third: "Both pass on one reading. But X's flat curve points to a steady leakage that one reading cannot show."

Screen 6, After the test: discharge. "When the test stops, the core is a charged capacitor. One core of String B has 0.528 µF. At 5 kV it holds Q = C × V = 0.528 × 10⁻⁶ × 5000 = 0.00264 C = 2.64 mC. Its energy is E = ½ × C × V² = 0.5 × 0.528 × 10⁻⁶ × 5000² = 6.60 J. Part of the charge has soaked into the insulation. It seeps back out after the core has been discharged, and can bring the voltage back." Then the order, which you never improvise: "Check the tester's display shows discharged. Then the discharge stick, then the hook stick, then the hand earth. Earth the core and the screen at both ends." Then the time: "Keep it discharging and earthed for at least five times as long as the test voltage was on.[^2] After a 1-minute spot reading, that is at least 5 minutes. Some older guidance says four times. Use five. Then leave the earths on until the next test needs them." The picture shows the five steps of the discharge as a strip of five cards, in order. Each card has a small drawing. They show the display reading discharged, the discharge stick, the hook stick, the hand earth, and earths on core and screen at both ends. Under it, a timeline drawn to scale shows a 1-minute spot reading, then 5 minutes earthed.

Screen 7, Worked example, a line at each press. "L3 at 5 kV reads 17.5 GΩ at 30 s, 23.0 GΩ at 1 minute and 60.0 GΩ at 10 minutes. These are practice values." The prompt: "Work each line yourself first, then press Show." Line 1: "DAR = R60s ÷ R30s = 23.0 ÷ 17.5 = 1.31. Satisfactory: 1.25 to 1.6.[^3]" Line 2: "PI = R10 ÷ R1 = 60.0 ÷ 23.0 = 2.61. Okay: 2 to 4.[^4]" Line 3: "The voltage held for the full 10 minutes, and 23.0 GΩ beats the client's 1 GΩ. L3 passes." Notes under the lines: "A DAR is done in 1 minute, where a PI takes 10. That makes it the quick check. It comes out lower than the PI. Its two readings are only 30 s apart, so it sees less of the climb." Then: "Makers draw the bands in other places. Some call a PI of 2.0 or more good,[^5] and a DAR of 1.4 or more.[^6] On those bands, L3's PI counts as good, but its DAR of 1.31 falls short. The client's test spec decides pass or fail." Then: "One more caution. Some insulation shows very little absorption, so its reading barely climbs even when it is sound.[^7] So read each core's PI beside its sister cores. The core that stands apart is the one to question." Read: L3's DAR is 23.0 ÷ 17.5 = 1.31, satisfactory. Its PI is 60.0 ÷ 23.0 = 2.61, okay. It held the voltage for 10 minutes and beats the client's 1 GΩ. So it passes. Still: all three lines are shown, with the notes.

Screen 8, Section A, question 3 (a). The scenario panel comes first. Then the test is set out once: "Each core of String B is tested in turn at 5 kV d.c., core to screen, for 10 minutes. The client asks for at least 1 GΩ at 1 minute. These are practice values. L1 reads 18.0 GΩ at 30 s, 24.0 GΩ at 1 minute and 62.0 GΩ at 10 minutes." The question: "(a) Determine the polarisation index of core L1." You type the answer for part 3a, with no unit: 62.0 ÷ 24.0 = 2.58, to 2 places. Slips: 0.39, "That is the ratio upside down. Put the 10-minute reading on top."; 1.33, "That is L1's DAR, 24.0 ÷ 18.0. PI uses the 1-minute and 10-minute readings."; 38.0, "That is the rise in GΩ. PI is a ratio, so divide." After two misses, the working. Then: "2.58 sits in 2 to 4, okay. L1's DAR is 24.0 ÷ 18.0 = 1.33, satisfactory. L3 works out at a PI of 2.61."

Screen 9, Section A, question 3 (b). Part (a) carried forward: 2.58. "L2 reads 2.10 GΩ at 30 s, 2.20 GΩ at 1 minute and 2.40 GΩ at 10 minutes. (b) Determine the polarisation index of core L2." You type the answer for part 3b, with no unit: 2.40 ÷ 2.20 = 1.09, to 2 places. Slips: 0.92, "That is the ratio upside down. Put the 10-minute reading on top."; 1.05, "That is L2's DAR, 2.20 ÷ 2.10. PI uses the 1-minute and 10-minute readings."; 0.20, "That is the rise in GΩ. PI is a ratio, so divide." After two misses, the working. Then a second question: "How does it rate, and would it go through?" Choices: "Okay. It beats 1 GΩ, so it goes through."; "Questionable. Record it and find out why first."; "Poor. It fails outright." Right, the second: "1.09 sits in 1 to 2, questionable. Its 1-minute reading of 2.20 GΩ beats the client's 1 GΩ. On that reading alone, L2 would have gone through. Its flat curve is what holds it back." Wrong, the first: "It does beat the client's 1 GΩ at 1 minute. But a PI of 1.09 sits in 1 to 2, questionable. One reading misses that flat curve." Wrong, the third: "Poor is below 1. A PI of 1.09 sits in 1 to 2, questionable." Then: "L2's DAR is 2.20 ÷ 2.10 = 1.05, inadequate. Set beside L1's 2.58 and L3's 2.61, L2's PI stands out. Most of L2's current is steady leakage. Record it, and find out why before you submit. The sheath test comes next."

On screens 8 to 10 a test record sits under the working, like the sheet on the job. Its columns are L1, L2 and L3, and its rows the readings at 30 s, 1 minute and 10 minutes, in GΩ, then DAR, PI and rating. L3's column is filled from the worked example. L1's ratios fill in once part (a) is answered, and L2's column once part (b) and its rating are.

Screen 10, Section A, question 3 (c). Parts (a) and (b) carried forward. "L2's PI test held 5 kV for 10 minutes. (c) Determine the least time L2 must then stay discharged and earthed." You type the answer for part 3c, in minutes: 5 × 10 = 50 min. Slips: 10, "That is how long the test ran. Allow five times that."; 40, "That is four times, an older rule. Allow five times." After two misses, the working. Then: "Keep the earths on L2's core and screen at both ends for at least 50 minutes. Leave them on until the next test needs them."

Screen 11, Section B: "Explain why a PI or DAR tells you more about a cable's insulation than a single IR reading." You write an answer, marked against five points. Any three make a full answer. You get one more go, then the model answer.

Screen 12, Section A, changed numbers. "Another cable's core reads 8.0 GΩ at 1 minute and 9.6 GΩ at 10 minutes. Determine its PI." You type the answer, with no unit: 9.6 ÷ 8.0 = 1.20. Slips: 0.83, "That is the ratio upside down. Put the 10-minute reading on top."; 1.6, "That is the rise in GΩ. PI is a ratio, so divide." Then: "1.20 sits in 1 to 2, questionable. Find out why before you submit it."

Screen 13, Keep this: the summary card, then Finish the lesson.

On the screens with working, a caption says each line is worked from the rounded figures shown before it. Each screen that uses a practice value says so.
interactive.ignores: The curves on screens 3 and 4 are a sketch, not String B's readings. They come from one simple rule with practice values, and every real cable has its own. The charging current is drawn as a spike in the first seconds. In fact it falls fast but never quite to nothing. Moisture is drawn as extra steady leakage only. Real water can change the absorption too. Halving for every 10 °C is a rule of thumb. Each insulation differs. Warmth also speeds up the absorption. So a real ratio moves a little with temperature, while the sketch's does not move at all. Current across the surface of the terminations is not shown. A guard terminal takes it out of the reading.

explain.text:
An IR test puts a steady d.c. voltage across the insulation and reads the current that gets through. On a long cable that current keeps falling for minutes, so the reading climbs. How far it climbs tells you more than where it starts. A ratio of two readings on the same cable, taken close together, measures that climb.

The current has three parts. A charging current fills the cable's capacitance and dies away in seconds. An [[absorption current]] flows while the insulation slowly polarises. Charge inside the plastic shifts into line with the field, and that slow shift is a current. It dies away over minutes. A leakage current runs through the insulation and stays. The tester shows voltage ÷ current. So the reading climbs as the first two fade. In dry, clean insulation the leakage is tiny, and the climb is steep. Water or dirt adds leakage that never fades. It swamps the absorption, and the curve stays flat.

A single reading also swings with temperature. Insulation resistance roughly halves for every 10 °C rise.[^1] The two readings in a ratio are taken close together, at the same temperature. Warmth pulls both down together, so the ratio barely moves. The [[polarisation index]], PI, is the 10-minute reading over the 1-minute one. The [[dielectric absorption ratio]], DAR, is the 60-second reading over the 30-second one. You may also see it called the dynamic absorption ratio. Both can show moisture that one passing reading hides. The sketches are simplified. Every cable has its own absorption and leakage. Some insulation shows very little absorption at all.

**A dry core's reading climbs as the charging and absorption currents fade. A wet core's stays flat. So on a long cable, a PI or DAR near 1 points to steady leakage. That holds even when the 1-minute reading passes.**

analogy.text: Think of charging a battery bank through an ammeter. The current starts high and tapers as the cells fill. What is left at the end is the bank's own leak. A healthy bank tapers to a small current. A bank with a fault keeps drawing a high current, and the taper is lost.
analogy.breaks: A battery stores its charge in chemistry and tapers over hours. Insulation tapers over minutes, as charge settles into the plastic. A cable's leak comes from water and dirt in the insulation. It gets worse as the cable warms.

practice.text:
- Before you start, check the circuit is disconnected and nothing else can see the test voltage. Make sure the cable is discharged. Restrict access at both ends. Use the maker's test leads only.
- Earth the core and the screen at both ends. Talk to the far end before every change.
- Connect red to the screen and black to the core. Red is the positive, so it sits on the earthed outside of the insulation.
- Lift the earths the test needs, under control. Run the test at the client's voltage. A PI needs 10 minutes. Note the readings at 30 s, 1 minute and 10 minutes.
- It passes if the voltage held for the full time and the resistance beats the client's figure. Where you can, take a PI or a DAR too.
- Work out DAR = R60s ÷ R30s and PI = R10 ÷ R1. Check each against its bands.
- Discharge in order: the display shows discharged, then the discharge stick, then the hook stick, then the hand earth. Earth the core and the screen at both ends.
- Keep it earthed for at least five times as long as the voltage was on. That is 50 minutes after a 10-minute PI.[^2] Leave the earths on until the next test needs them.

**The bands:** PI below 1 poor, 1 to 2 questionable, 2 to 4 okay, above 4 good.[^4] DAR below 1.25 inadequate, 1.25 to 1.6 satisfactory, above 1.6 excellent.[^3] Makers' tables draw the lines elsewhere. The client's test spec decides pass or fail.

**Rule of thumb:** a single reading roughly halves for every 10 °C rise. Only compare single readings taken at, or corrected to, the same temperature.

**Rule of thumb:** a DAR is done in 1 minute, where a PI takes 10. The DAR usually comes out lower than the PI. Its readings are only 30 s apart, so it sees less of the climb.

**Worked example:** L3 of String B at 5 kV reads 17.5 GΩ at 30 s, 23.0 GΩ at 1 minute and 60.0 GΩ at 10 minutes. These are practice values. DAR = 23.0 ÷ 17.5 = 1.31, satisfactory. PI = 60.0 ÷ 23.0 = 2.61, okay. The voltage held, and 23.0 GΩ beats the client's 1 GΩ. So L3 passes.

**Common mistakes**
- Passing a core on one reading that beats the client's figure, with a flat curve behind it.
- Working the ratio upside down. A healthy core's PI is above 1.
- Lifting the earths before the cable has had its full discharge time.
- Reading a PI of 1 to 2 on a short, low-capacitance run as a fault. Such a run shows very little absorption, so 1 to 2 is acceptable there.[^8]
- Comparing single readings taken at different temperatures.

b1.q: Explain why a PI or DAR tells you more about a cable's insulation than a single IR reading.

points.text: A single reading swings with temperature. Insulation resistance falls sharply as it warms, roughly halving for every 10 °C rise.

b1.model: A single IR reading swings with temperature. Insulation resistance roughly halves for every 10 °C rise. So a reading on a warm day can look worse with nothing wrong. PI and DAR compare two readings on the same cable, close together, at the same temperature. So the ratio barely moves. The ratio also shows how the current behaves. In dry, clean insulation the charging and absorption currents die away and leave a small leakage. So the reading climbs, and the ratio comes out well above 1. In wet or dirty insulation a high, steady leakage hides the absorption. So the curve stays flat, and the ratio sits near 1. A core can beat the client's figure on one reading and still show a flat curve. The ratio catches it.

summary.title: Insulation resistance: IR, DAR and PI
summary.for: Is the insulation dry and clean at low stress? Put a steady d.c. voltage between core and screen, and read it over 10 minutes.
summary.rule:
PI = R10min ÷ R1min
DAR = R60s ÷ R30s
Discharge: at least 5 × the time the voltage was on
Discharge order: display shows discharged, discharge stick, hook stick, hand earth, then earths on core and screen at both ends.
Q = C × V
E = ½ × C × V²

PI: below 1 poor, 1–2 questionable, 2–4 okay, above 4 good.
DAR: below 1.25 inadequate, 1.25–1.6 satisfactory, above 1.6 excellent.
Makers' bands differ: the client's spec decides.
Red to screen, black to core.
Near 1 is the bad end: the curve is flat.
One reading roughly halves for every 10 °C rise. A ratio barely moves.
